obtained.how: the publisher's own open-access full text (Taylor & Francis, Journal of Freshwater Ecology, gold OA), saved as HTML by the human (docs/research_notes/fetched/, 'Full article_ Modeling White Sucker …html') and indexed with getsrc --file; Table 1 read from the table data embedded in the same page

bibliography.checked_against: the article page header and Crossref
bibliography.note: Megan Begley, Stephen M. Coghlan Jr. & Joseph Zydlewski (University of Maine; USGS Maine Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit), 'Modeling White Sucker (Catostomus commersonii) populations to assess commercial harvest influence on age structure', J. Freshw. Ecol. 33(1): 413–428, published online 29 Nov 2018. Several of the values the paper cites are inputs this modelling paper takes from Begley, Coghlan & Zydlewski 2017 (N. Am. J. Fish. Manag. 37: 510–523), the field study of six Maine lakes.

claims.claim: Little Moxie Pond, Maine (30 ha; max 2.7 m), removal by depletion 1994–96: white sucker spawners ≈ 640/ha
claims.quote: computed as 19,141 spawning individuals for the Little Moxie Pond population
claims.conditions: MDIFW ten-year white sucker removal project (Tim Obrey, MDIFW, unpublished data, cited by the authors); pond area 0.30 km², maximum depth 2.7 m; trap-net catches 11,003, 7,100 and 188 in the first three years (from 1994); maximum-likelihood multiple-pass depletion estimate (Lockwood & Schneider 2000)
claims.note: 19,141 / 30 ha = 638/ha. The underlying data are unpublished MDIFW data reported by Begley et al.; the paper's 'one pond; a high end, project judgment' framing is fair.

claims.claim: mean FL at age 201–474 mm in three unfished Maine lakes
claims.location: web page, Methods (size at age and fecundity); Table 1 ('Length at age (age-3 to 21): 201–473 mm')
claims.quote: Average size at age (201-mm to 474-mm) was assigned based on the estimates provided by
claims.conditions: spawning adults (ages 3–21) from three Maine lakes closed to commercial harvest, n = 444, aged from transverse sections of lapillus otoliths; measurements from Begley et al. 2017; the text treats them as fork lengths ('Average fork length at age was used…')
claims.note: Table 1 prints 201–473 mm against the text's 201–474. The data are Begley et al. 2017's: cite 'Begley et al. 2017, via Begley, Coghlan & Zydlewski 2018', as the paper already does for the 26-yr age.

claims.claim: Maine males mature from age 2, females from age 3
claims.quote: mature females were first captured at age-3
claims.conditions: observations of Begley et al. 2017: reproductively mature migrating males as young as age 2 (< 2 % of the spawning run), mature females first at age 3 (3 % of the run)
claims.note: The model itself uses age 3 as first maturity for both sexes.

claims.claim: proportion mature 0.20, 0.30, 0.60 at ages 3–5, all from age 6 (presented with the Maine maturity data)
claims.source_value: model assumptions, not Maine measurements: P(age 4) = 0.30, P(age 5) = 0.60 and 1.00 from age 6 are taken from Wakefield & Beckman 2005; P(age 3) = 0.20 was set 'arbitrarily'; in the model each is further multiplied by a sequential-spawning probability of 0.65 (Geen et al. 1966) from age 4
claims.location: web page, Methods (maturity); Table 1 (Probability of spawning P, sources '–' and 4 = Wakefield and Beckman 2005)
claims.quote: we arbitrarily set P Age 3 at 0.20
claims.note: Write 'model values 0.20 (assumed), 0.30, 0.60 at ages 3–5, 1.0 from 6 (Wakefield & Beckman 2005, as used by Begley, Coghlan & Zydlewski 2018)'.

claims.location: web page, Methods (fecundity); Table 1 (a = 0.5214, b = 1.7541, source Begley et al. 2017)
claims.quote: the number of eggs produced per individual ranged from 3,910 to 26,060 eggs
claims.conditions: exponential fork length–fecundity relationship for Maine females (n = 437, Begley et al. 2017; R² = 0.57), applied to the model's mean length at each age 3–21; the authors call it possibly conservative against 5,000–59,000 reported elsewhere

claims.claim: Maine fish to 26 yr (Begley 2017, via Begley, Coghlan & Zydlewski 2018)
claims.quote: observed fish as old as twenty-six
claims.conditions: 'In Maine, Begley et al. (2017) observed fish as old as twenty-six'; the model caps age at 21 (other maximum ages reported: 21 and 23)
claims.note: 'Begley 2017' should be 'Begley et al. 2017' (Begley, Coghlan & Zydlewski 2017).

claims.claim: natural mortality M 0.97 at age 1, 0.25 thereafter
claims.location: web page, Methods (natural mortality); Table 1 (Natural mortality: YOY 0.97, Age-1 0.97, Age-2 to 21 0.25)
claims.quote: For the model we used age-1 fish M = 0.97
claims.conditions: instantaneous rates (converted to interval mortality in the model); literature-based inputs — 0.97 from McPhee 2007, 0.25 for ages 2–21 citing McPhee 2007, Miller et al. 2013 and Begley et al. 2017; the authors note that published M 'varies greatly among studies'
claims.note: Table 1 also applies 0.97 to young-of-year. These are model inputs, not a Maine estimate.

notes: Other values: average harvest mortality in Maine's fished lakes F = 0.466 (Begley et al. 2017); recruitment α = 0.0035 from Johnson 1975 (a 2.45-km² Minnesota lake); modelled unfished age structure dominated by ages 4–8 (~50 %), < 10 % aged 18+; under harvest ages 3–6 > 70 % of the run. Maine's white sucker bait fishery dates from 1991. For field values (size, age, fecundity, mortality) the primary is Begley, Coghlan & Zydlewski 2017, which is not in this batch.
